Metals.q: An unknown element is shiny, bends without breaking and conducts electricity. What is it most likely?
wrong: Nonmetals are brittle and poor conductors.
Metalloids have only some metallic properties; this one shows all of them.
Noble gases are gases, not shiny solids that bend.
Metals.exp: Shiny, bendable and conductive are metal properties.

Malleable.q: A gold bar is hammered into a sheet thinner than paper. Which property does this show?
wrong: Ductility is being drawn into wire, not hammered into sheets.
Conductivity is about carrying heat or electricity.
Malleable.exp: Being hammered or bent into shape is malleability.

Ductile.q: Copper is pulled through a die to make electrical wire. Which property makes that possible?
wrong: Malleability is being hammered into sheets, not drawn into wire.
A brittle material would snap instead of stretching.
Density has nothing to do with being drawn into wire.
Ductile.exp: Being drawn out into wire is ductility.

Nonmetals.q: Sulfur is yellow, shatters when struck and does not conduct electricity. Where is it on the table?
wrong: That is where the metals are; metals do not shatter.
Metalloids have some metallic properties; sulfur has none.
Those are the inner transition metals.
Nonmetals.exp: Brittle and nonconducting means nonmetal, right of the staircase.

Metalloids.q: Which element has some metallic and some nonmetallic properties?
wrong: Aluminum touches the staircase but is a metal.
Metalloids.exp: Silicon sits on the staircase: a metalloid.

Group.q: Why do lithium, sodium and potassium react in similar ways?
wrong: They are in different periods, so they have different numbers of shells.
Each element has a different number of protons.
Their atomic masses are very different.
Group.exp: Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons.

Alkali metals.q: Which element is an alkali metal?
wrong: Hydrogen sits in group 1 but is a nonmetal.
Magnesium is in group 2, the alkaline earth metals.
Alkali metals.exp: Potassium is in group 1, below hydrogen.

Alkaline earth metals.q: Strontium is in group 2. What charge does its ion have?
wrong: Only noble gases tend not to form ions.

Transition metals.q: Why might a question about iron's ion need to tell you its charge?
wrong: Iron does form ions: Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺.
Iron is a metal in the transition block.
Iron's charge varies; 1+ is the alkali metal charge.
Transition metals.exp: Transition metals in groups 3 to 12 often have variable charges.

Halogens.q: Bromine is a halogen. What ion does it form?
wrong: Halogens gain an electron; they do not lose one.
2- ions come from group 16, not group 17.
Only noble gases tend not to form ions.
Halogens.exp: Group 17 gains one electron to complete its octet.

Noble gases.q: Why does argon not form ions?
wrong: It has no electrons at all
Noble gases.exp: Group 18 already has a complete valence shell.

Boron, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen famil.q: Phosphorus is in group 15. Which family is that?
wrong: Families are named for the top element of the group, and phosphorus is not at the top.
Boron, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen famil.exp: Each family is named for the element at the top of its group.

Inner transition metals.q: Where are the inner transition metals on the periodic table?
wrong: That column is group 18, the noble gases.
That is the main transition metal block.
Inner transition metals.exp: They are the lanthanide and actinide rows set below the table.

Lanthanide series.q: Which atomic numbers make up the lanthanide series?
wrong: Those are group numbers for the transition metals.
Those are group numbers, not atomic numbers.

Actinide series.q: The actinide series is named after which element?
wrong: Uranium is in the series but does not name it.
There is no element called actinide.

Period.q: Sodium is in period 3. How many electron shells (energy levels) does it have?
wrong: 1 is its number of valence electrons (group 1).
8 is a full octet, not a shell count.
Period.exp: The period number gives the number of energy levels.

States at room temperature.q: At 25 °C, how many elements on the periodic table are liquids?
wrong: Two elements are liquids at room temperature.
That was Rutherford, about 2,300 years later.
Leucippus.exp: Leucippus and a partner proposed that matter is made of tiny particles.

Antoine Lavoisier.q: Wood burns and the ash weighs less, but nothing is truly lost. Whose idea explains this?
Antoine Lavoisier.exp: Lavoisier: matter is not created or destroyed, only changed in form.

Dalton's atomic theory (1810).q: In a reaction, the atoms are rearranged into new substances. Which theory says this?
wrong: Bohr's model is about where electrons are.
Thomson's model describes the inside of an atom, not reactions.
Heisenberg's work is about predicting electron positions.
Dalton's atomic theory (1810).exp: Dalton said atoms are not created or destroyed, only regrouped.

Law of constant composition.q: Water from a lake and water from a lab both have 2 H for every O. Which law is this?
wrong: That law is about mass not being created or destroyed.
That is about atoms not splitting in reactions.
That is about atoms completing their valence shells.
Law of constant composition.exp: A compound always has the same atoms in the same ratio.

J. J. Thomson (1897).q: Which discovery belongs to J. J. Thomson?
J. J. Thomson (1897).exp: Thomson used cathode ray tubes to find tiny negative particles.

Plum pudding model.q: In the plum pudding model, what are the 'plums'?
wrong: The positive charge is the pudding, spread throughout.
Neutrons had not been discovered yet.
The plum pudding model has no nucleus.
Plum pudding model.exp: Negative electrons were scattered in a ball of positive charge.

Ernest Rutherford (1911).q: Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil. What did Rutherford conclude?
wrong: Solid atoms would stop or bounce most particles.
Neutrons were found later by Chadwick.
Ernest Rutherford (1911).exp: Particles passing straight through means mostly empty space.

Nucleus.q: Where is almost all of an atom's mass?
wrong: Rutherford showed the mass is packed in a tiny center.
Nucleus.exp: Protons and neutrons, which have mass, are in the nucleus.

James Chadwick (1932).q: Chadwick's neutral radiation from beryllium turned out to be what?
wrong: Alpha particles were what he fired, not what he found.
James Chadwick (1932).exp: Neutral particles with about a proton's mass: neutrons.

Niels Bohr (1913).q: Which model shows electrons circling the nucleus like planets around the sun?
wrong: Thomson's model has no nucleus to circle.
Dalton's atoms had no inner parts.
Orbitals are likely regions, not planet-like paths.
Niels Bohr (1913).exp: Bohr placed electrons in fixed orbits.

Energy level.q: Chlorine is in period 3. How many energy levels does its Bohr model need?
wrong: 7 is chlorine's number of valence electrons.
Chlorine has more than one shell; period 3 means 3.
Energy level.exp: The period number gives the number of energy levels.

Problem with Bohr's model.q: What is wrong with Bohr's model of the atom?
wrong: It puts electrons in the nucleus
Bohr placed electrons outside the nucleus, in orbits.
Bohr's electrons are negative, as they should be.
Bohr's model includes protons in the nucleus.
Problem with Bohr's model.exp: We cannot know exactly where an electron is.

Orbitals (modern model).q: In the modern model, where is an electron found?
wrong: That is closer to Thomson's model.
Orbitals (modern model).exp: Orbitals are regions where an electron is likely to be about 90% of the time.

Proton.q: Which particle is positive and found in the nucleus?
wrong: Neutrons are in the nucleus but have no charge.
Electrons are negative and outside the nucleus.
An ion is a whole charged atom, not a particle inside one.

Neutron.q: Which particle is in the nucleus but has no charge?
wrong: Electrons are negative and outside the nucleus.
A cation is a positive ion, not a particle.

Electron.q: Which particle is nearly massless and found outside the nucleus?
wrong: Protons have mass and are in the nucleus.
Neutrons have mass and are in the nucleus.
The nucleus holds almost all the mass.

Number of protons.q: An atom gains a proton. What happens?
wrong: Ions form from gaining or losing electrons.
Isotopes differ in neutrons, not protons.
Changing protons changes the atomic number.
Number of protons.exp: The number of protons sets which element it is.

Number of electrons.q: Which change would affect how an atom bonds?
wrong: Neutrons make isotopes, which react almost the same.
Mass number counts nucleus particles, which do not bond.
Number of electrons.exp: Chemical behavior comes from the electrons.

Atomic number (Z).q: An atom has 26 protons. What is its atomic number?
wrong: That doubles the protons; atomic number is just the protons.
30 would be its neutron count for Fe-56, not its atomic number.
Atomic number (Z).exp: Atomic number = number of protons. 26 is iron.

Mass number (A).q: An atom has 11 protons and 12 neutrons. What is its mass number?

Neutron count.q: How many neutrons are in ³⁵₁₇Cl?

Electrons in a neutral atom.q: How many electrons are in a neutral magnesium atom (Z = 12)?
wrong: 10 is for Mg²⁺, which lost 2 electrons.
Electrons in a neutral atom.exp: Neutral atoms have as many electrons as protons.

Electrons in an ion.q: How many electrons are in O²⁻ (Z = 8)?
wrong: Subtracting 2 is for a positive ion; O²⁻ gained 2.
8 is for a neutral oxygen atom.

Valence electrons.q: Nitrogen is in group 15. How many valence electrons does it have?
wrong: Use the last digit of groups 13-18: group 15 means 5.
3 is how many it gains to form N³⁻.

Bohr model drawing.q: A Bohr model of magnesium (period 3, group 2) has how many rings and outer electrons?
wrong: Swapped: the period gives rings, the group gives outer electrons.
12 is the total electrons, not the outer ones.
There is one ring per energy level, not per electron.
Bohr model drawing.exp: Period 3 gives 3 rings; group 2 gives 2 valence electrons.

Octet.q: Why does chlorine gain one electron when it forms an ion?
wrong: Only H and He are complete with 2.
Gaining an electron makes it negative, not neutral.
Octet.exp: Chlorine has 7 valence electrons; one more completes the octet.

Atomic mass.q: Carbon's atomic mass is 12.011. Why isn't it exactly 12?
wrong: The decimal is real: it is a weighted average.
The decimal comes from the isotope mix.
Atomic mass.exp: Atomic mass is a weighted average of all of an element's isotopes.

Isotopes.q: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 have the same number of what?
Isotopes.exp: Isotopes have the same protons and different neutrons.

Chemistry of isotopes.q: Why do carbon-12 and carbon-14 react the same way?
wrong: They have different numbers of neutrons.
Charge is not what makes reactions alike; electrons are.
Chemistry of isotopes.exp: Chemistry depends on electrons, which isotopes share.

Isotopes in nature.q: Why is chlorine's atomic mass 35.45 and not a whole number?
Isotopes in nature.right: It is a mix of isotopes
wrong: Every atom has a whole number of neutrons.
Then its mass would be close to 35.0.
Isotopes in nature.exp: Natural chlorine is a mixture of isotopes.

Hydrogen isotopes.q: How many neutrons are in tritium (hydrogen-3)?

Isotopic notation.q: In ¹⁴₆C, what does the 6 tell you?
wrong: The mass number is the top number, 14.
Charge goes at the upper right; there is none here.
Isotopic notation.exp: The bottom number is the atomic number: protons.

Hyphen notation.q: How is ⁴¹₂₀Ca written in hyphen notation?
wrong: 20 is the atomic number; hyphen notation uses the mass number.

Same element test.q: Which pair is the same element?
wrong: Same mass number but different atomic numbers.
Different atomic numbers mean different elements.
Different atomic numbers mean different elements.
Same element test.exp: Same bottom number (Z = 7) means same element.

Relative (percent) abundance.q: Boron is 80% boron-11. What does the 80% mean?
wrong: Abundance is a share of atoms, not a mass.
Abundance is about how common, not how stable.
Relative (percent) abundance.exp: Abundance is how common each isotope is.

Weighted average atomic mass.q: Element X is 90% X-20 and 10% X-22. Which average mass makes sense?
wrong: That is a plain average; X-20 is far more common.
That treats X-22 as the common one.
That adds the masses without weighting.

Isotopic mass.q: In the Candium lab, what did the average mass of one candy type stand for?
wrong: Atomic number is a proton count, not a mass.
The total mixes every type together.
The lab measured masses, not particles.
Isotopic mass.exp: Each candy type was an isotope with its own mass.

Ion.q: An atom has 11 protons and 10 electrons. What is it?
wrong: Neutral atoms have equal protons and electrons.
Isotopes differ in neutrons, not electrons.
The protons (11, sodium) did not change.
Ion.exp: Unequal protons and electrons make an ion: Na⁺.

Cation.q: Calcium loses two electrons. What does it become?
wrong: Losing electrons makes it positive, not negative.
Isotopes differ in neutrons, not electrons.
It has 2 more protons than electrons now.
Cation.exp: Losing electrons makes a positive ion.

Anion.q: Sulfur gains two electrons. What does it become?
Anion.exp: Gaining electrons makes a negative ion.

Why atoms ionize.q: Why does sodium give up an electron to chlorine?
wrong: Na⁺ has a full shell but is still sodium.
Losing an electron makes it slightly lighter.
Why atoms ionize.exp: Na loses 1, Cl gains 1, and both reach complete outer shells.

Metals lose, nonmetals gain.q: Potassium and fluorine react. Which one loses electrons?
wrong: Fluorine is a nonmetal; it gains electrons.
One must lose and one must gain.
An ionic bond forms by transfer.
Metals lose, nonmetals gain.exp: Metals lose electrons; nonmetals gain them.

Group 1 and group 2 charges.q: What is the formula of the ion barium forms?
wrong: 1+ is for group 1; barium is in group 2.
Gallium is a metal, so it loses electrons.
Nitrogen is a nonmetal; it gains electrons.

Noble gas charge.q: Which element is least likely to form an ion?
Noble gas charge.exp: Neon's valence shell is already full.

Transition metal charges.q: Which element's ion charge must be given in a problem?
Transition metal charges.exp: Transition metals like iron have variable charges.

Bond.q: What happens to electrons when two atoms form a bond?
wrong: Electrons are not destroyed in a bond.
Bond.exp: A bond is the sharing or giving and taking of electrons.

Ionic bond.q: What holds Na⁺ and Cl⁻ together in table salt?
wrong: Each ion keeps its own nucleus.
Ionic bond.exp: The electrostatic attraction between a cation and an anion.

Covalent compound.q: Which pair of elements would form a covalent compound?
wrong: A metal and a nonmetal form an ionic compound.
Calcium is a metal, so this is ionic.
Lithium is a metal, so this is ionic.

Chemical formula.q: How many oxygen atoms are in one unit of Al₂O₃?
wrong: 2 is the number of aluminum atoms.
5 is the total number of atoms.

Ionic formula rule.q: Is MgCl a correct formula? Why or why not?
wrong: Order is right, but the charges must cancel too.
The metal does go first; the problem is the charge.

Crossover method.q: Use the crossover method for Al³⁺ and O²⁻. What is the formula?
wrong: The charges were not crossed: each ion takes the other's number.
+3 and -2 do not cancel one to one.
That reduces wrong; Al₂O₂ has +6 and -4.

Polyatomic ion.q: Why is Ca(CN)₂ written with parentheses?
wrong: The 2 applies only to what is inside the parentheses.
Ca(CN)₂ is ionic; parentheses group the ion.
Charges are not written in the formula.
Polyatomic ion.exp: The 2 means two whole CN⁻ ions.

Properties of ionic compounds.q: Solid salt does not conduct electricity, but salt water does. Why?
Properties of ionic compounds.exp: Dissolved or melted, the ions are free to move.

Molar mass.q: What is the molar mass of water, H₂O? (H = 1.008, O = 16.00)

Molar mass with subscripts.q: In CaCl₂, how many times do you add chlorine's mass?
wrong: The subscript 2 means two Cl atoms.
3 is the total number of atoms.
Chlorine is part of the formula.
Molar mass with subscripts.exp: Multiply Cl's mass by its subscript, 2.

Molar mass with parentheses.q: How many oxygen atoms are in one unit of Ca(NO₃)₂?
wrong: The 2 outside the parentheses doubles the 3 inside.
That adds 3 and 2 instead of multiplying.
2 is the number of NO₃ groups.

Mole.q: You have 1 mole of water molecules. How many molecules is that?
wrong: 18.02 is the mass of a mole in grams, not a count.
A mole is a huge count, not one particle.
3 is the atoms in one molecule.

Avogadro's number.q: How many atoms are in 2.00 mol of copper?
wrong: That divides by 2 instead of multiplying.

Grams to moles.q: How many moles are in 36.04 g of water (18.02 g/mol)?
wrong: That divides molar mass by grams.
That is the molar mass, not the moles.

Subscript ratio.q: How many moles of H atoms are in 3 mol of CH₄?
wrong: That is the moles of CH₄, not H.
That is per 1 mol of CH₄.
Subscript ratio.exp: 3 mol × 4 H per CH₄ = 12 mol H.

Roadmap to atoms.q: To go from grams of a compound to number of atoms, what comes first?
wrong: That comes last, after moles of atoms.
That comes after you have moles.
That only finds the molar mass.
Roadmap to atoms.exp: Grams → moles → moles of atoms → atoms.

Formula unit.q: Why do we count NaCl in formula units, not molecules?
wrong: NaCl has two ions per unit.
Molecules are covalent; NaCl is ionic.
Formula unit.exp: Ionic compounds are counted in formula units.
